title: Fix for problem with aaply in plyr >= 1.8.0
description:
## Problem running code from the J Stat Soft paper

When attempting to try out the examples from the [J Stat Soft](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v040i01) paper on plyr ("split-apply-combine" paradigm), the first examples with aaply and the ozone dataset failed.

I went back and rebuilt R from September 2009, and plyr from 2009, and tested the code as described in the paper and it all worked.  I then went through the various versions of plyr/R until the aaply code broke, which happened at plyr-1.8.0 (it is still broken when tested on the latest code from github).

After forking the plyr git repository, I have fixed the issue so that the ozone examples now work 
(without breaking the other 'testthat' tests).

Specifically, the changes are
- Added a new unit test to check that aaply works with an array list object
- Fixed the list_to_array code called by laply to correctly check whether or not the 'res' object (from llply) is from an array list, and deal with it appropriately.
- Checked that the new tests worked with the modified code, and that no other tests failed as a result of the new code.

Best 
Rob Pollock.

title: FIX: Keep .progress="progressr" even when .parallel=TRUE
description:
I'm aware that **plyr** is deprecated and AFAIU will only be kept on life support. 

However, if there's the slightest chance I can catch you in a weak moment, this teeny PR makes **dplyr** report on progress also when `.parallel = TRUE`. For this to work, one needs to use **doFuture** for parallel processing and **progressr** for progress managing (any progress reporter can be used, e.g. **progress**).  The only thing that prevents this to work out of the box is that **plyr** 1.8.6 forces `.progress = "none"` whenever `.parallel = TRUE`; this PR allows `.progress = "progressr"` through.

Example of `progress::progress_bar()` updates when running in parallel:

```r
>library(plyr)
> library(progressr)
> doFuture::registerDoFuture()
> future::plan("multisession", workers = 2L)
> handlers("progress")  ## 'progress' package

> with_progress({
+   y <- llply(1:10, function(x) { Sys.sleep(1); identity(x) },
+                 .parallel = TRUE, .progress = "progressr")
+ })
[================>---------------------------------------]  20%
```

Even if this PR never makes it in, I'll leave it here for future references, e.g. in case someone else revives this package.

title: Avoid length check errors
description:
The `llply` function doesn't accept a `.progress` argument other than names when the environment variables `_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_` is set (to a true-ish value). See [R Internals](https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-devel/R-ints.html).  This environment variables is apparently now set by Bioconductor.

If you supply the output of one of the progress_* function, `llply` fails with an error.

Steps to reproduce: 

    Sys.setenv(`_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_`="true")

    library(plyr)
    x <- list(a = 1:10, beta = exp(-3:3), logic = c(TRUE,FALSE,FALSE,TRUE))
    llply(x, mean, .progress=progress_text())

Yields the following error message: 

    Error in .progress == "none" && !.inform : 
      'length(x) = 3 > 1' in coercion to 'logical(1)'

Other plyr functions are unaffected and the progress_* functions work fine even with `_R_CHECK_LENGTH_1_LOGIC2_`  set.

This PR fixes the bug by first checking if .progress is of length 1.

title: rbind.fill should respect empty data frames
description:
``` R
> df1 <- data.frame(x = 1:2, y = 2:3)
> df2 <- data.frame(y = 3:4, z = 5:6)
```

rbind.fill with inputs that are empty data frames returns NULL instead of a data frame. rbind has the more consistent behavior, returning an empty data frame with the same columns as input:

``` R
> rbind.fill(subset(df1, FALSE))
NULL
> rbind(subset(df1, FALSE))
[1] x y
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```

I think rbind.fill should have behavior like rbind. If the output from rbind.fill is passed along to further computations, is is more likely for those further computations to successfully "do nothing" if the output is the expected type of data.frame and the expected columns are present.

To be consistent with the above, I think that this should return a data frame with a column Z that is filled with NA.

``` R
> rbind.fill(df1, subset(df2, FALSE))
  x y
1 1 2
2 2 3
```

And this should return a data frame with zero rows and columns "x", "y", "z". 

``` R
rbind.fill(subset(df1, FALSE), subset(df2, FALSE))
```

title: join and match_df don't match string to factor
description:
``` bash
dfF <- data.frame(character=c("Aeryn", "Jothee", "Jothee", "Chiana", "Scorpius", "Scorpius"),
                 species=c("Sebacian", "Luxan", "Sebacian", "Nibari", "Sebacian", "Scarran"))
dfS <- colwise(as.character)(dfF)

matchF <- data.frame(species="Sebacian", stringsAsFactors=TRUE)
matchS <- colwise(as.character)(matchF)

#"merge" matches strings to factors both directions
merge(dfF, matchS) #matches
merge(dfS, matchF) #matches

#as does '=='
dfF$species == matchS$species #matches
dfS$species == matchF$species #matches

#`match_df` doesn't match a string to a factor
match_df(dfF, matchF) #matches (despite having different level sets)
match_df(dfF, matchS) #matches string to factor
match_df(dfS, matchS) #matches string to string
match_df(dfS, matchF) #NO MATCHES for factor to string

#nor does `join`, (so inner joins are not commutative)
join(dfF, matchS, type="inner") #matches
join(dfS, matchF, type="inner") #NO MATCHES
```

I think this is a bug since `match_df` is supposed to match like `==` and we expect inner joins to be commutative up to an ordering.

title: rbind.fill performance and consistency improvements
description:
This is a substantial refactoring of `rbind.fill` that improves performance for combining large numbers of groups and improves consistency of behavior for different column types.
- Avoid inducing array copies for primitive/list types, ensuring linear performance (fixes #148).
- Special handling for `factor` and `POSIXct` types to avoid copying and ensure linear performance in those cases as well.
- Dims are handled independently of type and other attributes; factor-arrays, char-arrays and list-arrays are supported.
- Arrays of any dimension are supported.
- Colnames of matrix columns are preserved (like `rbind`.)
- Factor columns `rbind`ed to other data types are coerced to character.
- Consequently `match_df` and `join` handle combinations of character and factor on the index column (fixes #128).

Supporting performance measurements here: http://crowding.github.io/plyr/rbind-fill.html

![performance over revisions](http://crowding.github.io/plyr/figure-plot-rev.svg)

title: performance improvements for rbind.fill

The test tests the run time of `rbind.fill` for different list sizes and fits several linear models to check whether the dependence is O(n), O(n log n) or O(n^2). It runs in just a few seconds. These are the test results on my machine:

```

4   50  2     0.016    0.000   0.021          0         0  50  195.6012   2500
5  100  1     0.028    0.028   0.056          0         0 100  460.5170  10000
```

title: *aply does not rbind a list of lists
description:
With a list of numeric vectors, *aply will rbind the results together:

``` R
Browse[1]> dput(laply(list(c(1,2), c(3,4), c(5,6)), identity))
structure(c(1, 3, 5, 2, 4, 6), .Dim = c(3L, 2L), .Dimnames = list(NULL, c("1", "2")))
```

Whereas if the results are lists, *aply does not attempt to rbind them, even though it could:

``` R
Browse[1]> dput(laply(list(list(1,2), list(3,4), list(5,6)), identity))
structure(list(list(1, 2), list(3, 4), list(5, 6)), .Dim = 3L, .Dimnames = list(NULL))
```

Per the laply help, each element of list input should become a row of the output. Also per the help, laply's output should be similar to the transpose of sapply, which does what seems like the right thing in this case:

``` R
Browse[1]> dput(t(sapply(list(list(1,2), list(3,4), list(5,6)), identity)))
structure(list(1, 3, 5, 2, 4, 6), .Dim = c(3L, 2L))
```

title: First try at fix for scoping issues
description:
This is an attempt at a fix for #3.

It seems to do the right thing for the example code:

```
# Generate some data
set.seed(321)
myD <- data.frame( 
  Place = sample(c("AWQ","DFR", "WEQ"), 10, replace=T),
  Light = sample(LETTERS[1:2], 15, replace=T),
  value=rnorm(30) 
)

myfunc <- function(xdf, sctype) {
  force(sctype)
  ddply(xdf, .(Place, Light), transform, 
    rng = paste(value, sctype))
}

myfunc(myD, "range")
```

It also fixes the behavior for this question on stackoverflow: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6955128/object-not-found-error-with-ddply-inside-a-function

Some notes:
- It passes all the tests! (And it could probably use some new ones)
- I don't know how performance is with `do.call` vs. calling the function directly. 
- I've only implemented it for `ddply`, `ldply`, and `llply`.
- It's not implemented for the special "split" case in `llply`.

title: replace_values function
description:
This adds a function to replace values in a factor or character vector with new values. Examples:

``` R
x <- c("a", "b", "c")
replace_values(x, c("a" = "A", "c" = "C"))
# [1] "A" "b" "C"

y <- factor(c("a", "b", "c", "a"))
replace_values(y, c(a = "A", c = "C"))
# [1] A b C A
# Levels: A b C
```

It can be used for data frame column names, or list item names.

``` R
df <- data.frame(a=1, b=2, c=3)
names(df) <- replace_values(names(df),  c(a = "A", c = "C"))
df
# A b C
#1 2 3

lst <- list(a=1, b=2, c=3)
names(lst) <- replace_values(names(lst),  c(a = "A", c = "C"))
str(lst)
# List of 3
#  $ A: num 1
#  $ b: num 2
#  $ C: num 3
```

It's called in a manner similar to the `rename` function. One drawback to doing it this way, with named values, is that it won't work with numeric vectors. It could be done, but it would be a bit ugly, with a conversion to character vector in the middle. Also, this might be unpredictable for floating point values.

title: Preserve class/attributes in *dply
description:
Hi Hadley,

I can imagine you don't have more time for plyr than for ggplot at the moment, but just in case... Here is a weird behaviour (probably a bug) that I noticed when dealing with circular data or dates in ddply.

```
# let us create a data.frame with columns which have special classes
library("circular")
d = data.frame(a=round(runif(10)), 
    # dates, in POSIXct
    b=as.POSIXct(runif(10)*1000, origin="2011-01-01"),
    # circular data, of class "circular" and with numerous attributes
    c=circular(runif(10)))
llply(d, class)

# test a basic function
class(mean(d$b))
class(mean(d$c))
# it preserves POSIX and circular classes

# try to apply this function through ddply
class(ddply(d, ~a, function(x) mean(x$b))[,2])
class(ddply(d, ~a, function(x) mean(x$c))[,2])
# the results are only numeric

l = split(d, d$a)
class(llply(l, function(x) mean(x$b))[[1]])
class(llply(l, function(x) mean(x$c))[[1]])
# here classes are preserved

class(ldply(l, function(x) mean(x$b))[,2])
class(ldply(l, function(x) mean(x$c))[,2])
# here they are not, so the transformation into a data.frame is problematic

class(ldply(l, function(x) data.frame(mean(x$b)))[,2])
# here they are
# so the problem is when list_to_dataframe is given an atomic vector
```

A way to fix this is to transform those vectors into data.frames and treat them as such in the following (rbind them etc.). But converting a vector into a line of data.frame while conserving classes and attributes is surprisingly tricky. My implementation uses a for loop which is probably a bad start. But at least it works: the output always has the correct class.

title: Issue Fix 18
description:
This is a fix for plyr issue 18. 

The case for `length(.variables)==1` was already being handled in `splitter_d`, but without setting the `n` attribute as was expected. The unset `NULL` attribute was passed to split_indices, overriding what would have been the correct default value of `max(group)`.

http://github.com/hadley/plyr/issues#issue/18
